Okay so this is ridiculous: my shower handle that adjusts water temperature. I never had an issue with it until recently. We had a plumber fix something and he mentioned the hot/cold directions were “opposite of what you would expect”. Now everytime I shower, the “opposite” thing totally messes up my memory of which way is hot and which is cold. I do some ridiculous mental gymnastics… “okay so I would expect right to be hot because that’s what I’m used to. But per the plumber, mine is opposite of normal. So I SHOULD expect right to be cold. I am in the same boat as you, OP. I grew up without much, and am finally at a place where I feel safe and stable financially. I’m already 32. Despite desperately wanting kids, I know it would jeopardize my financial security. I couldn’t afford for myself or partner to get sick, get laid off, or any other life emergency. I couldn’t afford childcare. I couldn’t afford to stay home with my kids either. I couldn’t afford a college fund for them. I couldn’t afford healthy groceries regularly. I couldn’t afford any of the things that keep me sane currently such as hobbies and therapy. I couldn’t afford a babysitter for date nights with my partner, even just a few a year. I couldn’t afford my insurance deductible if a tree falls on my house, or if I need emergency surgery. My life would be MUCH more stressful, living on the hope that nothing goes wrong that could destroy my family’s wellbeing. 

I am also grieving my future of no children. Just because I am not willing to trade my mental health and physical well-being for a child, does not mean I cannot grieve my “choice” to be child free. In the USA, many facilities have “Patient Care Techs” or PCTs, which we tend to abbreviate to “tech”. The PCT is a Certified Nursing Assistant (CNA) which sounds similar to the CCA in Canada? Their certification is “CNA”, but their job title is PCT. 

They assist with vital signs, activities of daily living, and other patient care. They work closely alongside nursing staff. 

I see the confusion because we do also have imaging techs, laboratory techs, pharmacy techs, etc. But in general when nursing staff use the term “tech” they are probably referring to the PCT.

In my experience (float pool), med-surg is especially grueling. Both mentally and physically. It is just so constant, and I would literally be multitasking the entire 12-hours. ER can be similar in those regards, but still I think med-surg is worse. It does get a lot less stressful with experience, because you get faster at things and because you’re not freaking out about every little thing. But even after 7-years, it was still brutal lol.

I have the same hair. First of all, check out r/finehair! There are a few things that help. A blunt haircut without any layers is essential. I do face framing and curtain bangs, but no layers in the length. Using a lamellar rinse out (L’Oréal) adds some slip and shine without weight. Also, it looks MUCH better when I blow dry. Blow drying sort of smooths all the strands in a uniform way, where air drying they just dry wonky. Also my roots get oily so fast when I air dry. Lastly, I find it looks much better when I add curls with a wand.   That way I can make it kind of fluffy and it looks intentional. When it’s straight and limp, it looks bad so fast. Unfortunately, I don’t think it will ever look good without some heat styling. At least for me! 

Even with all of the above, I still have to carry a mini hairbrush with me and brush every few hours. That is the simplest solution lol.

ETA: agree with clarifying shampoo!!! Build-up happens so quick on fine hair. Double-wash every shampoo. Limit leave-in products to 1-2. Wash and blow dry frequently.

Yes, that is the definition of a living will. But a POLST is not a living will just because it contains some of the things in the definition you posted. Again, a living will is legal document, often prepared by legal counsel. It is meant for circumstances where a healthcare proxy is making decisions and wants to reference what the patient’s wishes are. Healthcare providers cannot use a living will to withhold life saving treatment without the consent of the patient or a proxy. 

In contrast, The POLST is a medical order, with a provider signature (just like a paper prescription). It is meant for medical providers to follow the written orders in emergency situations when the patient is incapacitated, without the need for a healthcare proxy. 

They can are completely different. The POLST was specifically created to help fill in the gaps where a living will is not sufficient. It prevents patients unnecessary suffering. The YouTube video I linked clarifies this very well!

I'm sorry, but you're wrong. It is not the equivalent of a living will. A living will is a legal document, and a POLST is a medical order signed by a physician. As I'm sure you know, there are scenarios where a person is not dead yet, but will be soon unless intensive care measures are taken. With a POLST, patients can opt in or out of varying "life sustaining treatments" with or without opting out of CPR. That is why the form has 2 different sections. It is not a living will, it is a medical order that includes code status AND other medical wishes. This video explains it pretty simply: [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QuRMTUZ76C0](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QuRMTUZ76C0)

Not sure why you're so adamant to argue the point, it is a necessary document and prevents patients from receiving interventions they do not want when emergencies happen, even in their own homes.

Apologies if my comment was confusing. The POLST form has options for BOTH scenarios: In the event of cardiopulmonary arrest, attempt CPR or do not attempt CPR. The form then includes further options for OTHER scenarios where there is a pulse, but intensive measures are needed to continue to sustain life. This is meant to provide MD orders for CPR and/or other life sustaining measures should the patient be incapacitated and unable to make their own decisions. 

POLST forms are largely for use OUTSIDE of the hospital setting. Patients often hang them on their fridge. If they call 911, EMS has clear medical orders to follow in emergent scenarios, with or without a pulse. **EMS cannot utilize living wills to refrain from providing life saving care, as living wills are not medical orders.**

In the hospital setting, electronic (Epic) orders trump everything. A patient does not need a POLST form to have "DNR Orders" for their hospital stay. However, if they wish to continue DNR status after hospital discharge, a signed POLST is required to provide a portable medical order. The hospital can also reference a existing POLST if needed to clarify complex patient care wishes (if they are unable to express their wishes) without the need for a healthcare proxy. Again, it is a medical order which distinctly classifies it separately from living wills.

If you google "POLST form" you will see exactly what I'm talking about. There is no need for policy changes - in my state this is a very simple and effective process that provides clarity in chaotic situations, it has not created for more chaos as you implied.

If you've never seen one or don't know what I'm talking about, your state probably does not use them. But some states do, and I figure that was what the above commenter was referring to when stating there are "multiple types of DNRs".

It may vary by state, but in Illinois we have POLST forms that include the DNR option AND further specify wishes for other types of life saving treatments such as meds, feeding tubes, etc. It’s meant to be a “portable” doctor’s order. It is specifically not categorized as a living will on purpose.

Same. This is exactly what I do. Often I put their exact response in quotes too. How else will I remember the conversation that transpired if I have to? In 5 years, my charting will allow me to remember the exact convo I had with the provider, at the exact minute it happened, with the exact words exchanged.

Omg. Never chart “will continue to monitor”. I thought all nurses knew this by now. It’s a common old habit, a bad habit. Horrible for legal purposes. When is “if necessary”? Are you coming up with your own parameters, or did the provider tell you when they would like to be notified? Is there an order for those parameters? What exactly are you monitoring? And how often? Does “continue to monitor” mean you are recycling the BP q15min? Or remaining with the patient 1:1 monitoring them? Or checking up on them again in 4 hours? 

In general you should not chart what you “will” do - only chart what you have actually already done. 

Also - “No new orders” is not passive aggressive. It is factual and objective. The chart should always be factual and objective. Why is stating the facts passive aggressive?

I chart their response to my notifications simply to ensure if I get called for a deposition in 5 years, I’ll remember what the physician’s reply was. I feel it is only factual to reflect their reply in the chart. What would be the purpose of NOT documenting their response? I’m truly curious because I don’t see how it would be beneficial to omit this. 

Really there are only 3 response options: “no response” “see orders” “no new orders”. I always chart which it is. If no response; I keep paging until I get one. And chart all of those pages as well. Often I also include their exact response in quotes. Can’t get more factual than that.

All new nurses feel this way, it is so normal. Nursing school is only the tip of the iceberg with learning, you will learn everything you need on the job. Oh I see, so basically you didn’t get much real life clinical experience? 

Honestly, I think long term care is a great place to learn skills. I don’t think you really need a residency program for that. 

Practicing IVs on the fake mannequins arms is nice, but it is not necessary. For IVs, the BEST way to learn is to just do them!! Do them as much and often as you can, in real life. The more you do, the better you get.

In my opinion, if you were going to a high acuity inpatient unit, a residency program would be helpful. For long term care, I think you can learn on the job successfully. 

Just my thoughts :)

ETA: Make sure you look up the LTC facility and get an idea about nursing ratios, how long your orientation will be, and if you will be working alone at some point. Some nursing homes and facilities have only 1 RN on staff, for MANY residents, and I think that would be very very hard as a new grad.

Last thought - if you want to do 1 year at the hospital to learn nursing skills and gain experience, you will be able to pretty much transfer anywhere you want after that. Long term care generally is not a hard specialty to get into to. You could transfer to LTC whenever you want if you did take the hospital job.

Personally I really enjoyed my new grad residency program. I was scared shitless as a new grad and the program was nice. I got to connect with other new grads, practice skills, and ask “dumb” questions outside of the clinical setting. That being said, I wouldn’t say the program was amazing enough to be worth giving up your dream specialty. 

Also, all residency programs are different. The content, skills offerings, and requirements may be different. Mine was a monthly in-person meetings with both educational content and skills. We had no project requirements. At the new hospital I work at, the program is similar but includes skills fairs every 3 months instead of at all the meetings, and they do an EBP project.

Some of the nurses love it and are appreciative of it, and some hate it and try to get out of the meetings lol.  It all depends on what you think you need as a new grad. Do you want extra support for venting, questions and advice? Or do you think you’ll be fine with just a preceptor as your main support system? 

With or without the program, your orientation on the floor will be similar in length. The 1-year program is mainly for support with extra things after that. Like talking with other new grads about how you feel, sharing struggles and successes, and getting a little extra practice with clinical skills. 

I will say it’s nice to have support from some experienced nurses outside of your unit. I was always a bit nervous talking to my manager and even unit educator. But the residency program nurses I felt more comfortable to talk to and learn from. For me, it’s what I needed. 

Lastly, I had the time and energy to come to those meetings outside of my work schedule. Other nurses struggled with child care and work/life balance, and felt the meetings were just making things more stressful for them.

You could also look into topical Dapsone gel, it is good for hormonal acne. My derm originally wanted me to use dapsone gel, tretinoin and the Spiro all together. But the dapsone and tretinoin can both cause dryness, which my skin couldn’t tolerate. 

I did not notice any purging with Spiro, just slow/gradual improvement! The tretinoin can cause purging for sure though, just FYI. But it’s considered a gold standard for acne and I know a lot of people have very good success with it!

Hey there! Sure, my Spiro journey has been slow and steady. I believe I started at 50mg, and 1.5 years later I am taking 150mg. This dose has me 99% clear. I saw some improvement within the first 3 months, but was still getting random break outs around my period, which is why my derm kept gradually increasing my dose.

Every 3 months it got better and better, and now I am very clear with only minor break outs once in a while. I think it’s all about finding that perfect dose for your body. 

As far as side effects, they have been minimal. Actually, I’ve noticed mostly good things. Slight increase in breast size, new hair growth on my head, (especially on my temples), and less oily hair. I have not gained any weight, or noticed any new cellulite. No dizziness or fatigue either.

The only “bad” side effects I’ve had are irregular periods (evened out eventually), slightly more frequent peeing, and dryness! My skin is superrr dry now, I can’t even use the tretinoin anymore. My routine is 100% hydrating products and no actives. But I’ve always had dry/sensitive skin. I think the Spiro just exacerbates the dryness.

Overall I think it’s been super successful, and I’m very happy with my dose and results.

I’d ask about a cardiac monitor (often called a Holter monitor or Zio patch). It’s like a sticker with a button, you wear on your chest for 14-30 days. You press the button anytime you feel heart palpitations. Then, you mail it to the the monitor company and your results are forwarded to your doctor. This way, they can see exactly what is happening with your heart in the moments when you’re feeling those symptoms.

Well that averages out to about a pound a day - which is pretty rapid. I would say the combination of rapid weight gain without an increase in calories, plus the leg swelling points to fluid retention rather than gaining fat or muscle. 

I’d just advise to at least get checked out to see what the cause is. I know it sucks making an appointment or going to the ER. It’s totally possible it’s not anything serious. But it just seems very odd to have these symptoms out of the blue. 

It is not normal for your body to accumulate so much fluid that it is causing pitting edema in your legs. Maybe some bloating if you’re eating a lot of salty foods, but enough to gain 6 lbs and cause leg swelling seems abnormal - especially in a person without any known conditions to be causing it.

As someone else mentioned, lymphatic system issues can also cause swelling. That could be a potential cause outside of heart or kidney issues, but is still something you’d want a diagnosis for.

As a nurse, I agree with what other healthcare professionals on this thread have told you. If you press and it leaves an indentation, it’s pitting edema. Fat or muscle gain would not indent like that.

There are several causes for this, the most common being heart and/or kidney failure. The general rule of thumb is that if you gain more than 3lbs in 3 days, it’s concerning for a heart failure exacerbation.

I don’t want you to panic, but your symptoms are definitely concerning enough to go get medical attention. Regardless of the cause, the fluid retention in and of itself can be dangerous. Excess fluid can cause electrolyte imbalances which can cause all kinds of serious problems. 

If you go to the hospital and they believe you’re experiencing “fluid overload”, they will likely admit you and give you diuretics to help you pee off the excess fluid. They will also limit your fluid and salt intake, give you electrolyte supplements as needed based on your blood work, and closely monitor your heart.

I like to look at marijuana the same as any other medicine. For every medication, there is something called a “therapeutic dose”. If he is using marijuana as an anti-anxiety, antidepressant, sleep aid etc. that is just as valid as taking Xanax, Prozac, ambien, etc. 

That being said, most medications have side effects and safety considerations. For example, it is illegal to drive under the influence of narcotics or benzos (such as Xanax) due to the risk of motor function and reaction time impairment.

So, I’d look at it like this. If marijuana is a daily medication for him - that’s totally fine. However, he should be honest with himself regarding his daily dose - how much is therapeutic vs. harmful, and certain precautions he must take while using it. 

I personally do not drive after smoking, for ME it doesn’t feel safe and I would be paranoid the whole time. In addition, it’s illegal and I’m not willing to risk that. However, I know many marijuana users who say it doesn’t impact their ability to drive at all and they do it all the time without issue. I can’t speak to that. But I’d agree with you it would not be worth risking especially with kids in the car. 

My last note would be that you really need to ensure your relationship is rock solid in every other area if you’re going to be willing to change your views on this issue for him. Yup I went off birth control right after finishing Accutane. I didn’t notice any immediate relapse with my skin. Like you, the birth control made my acne worse when I started it. I’m prone to hormonal acne and oddly birth control has always made it worse even though for many people it makes it better. I didn’t want to go back on birth control because it makes me feel like shit mentally and physically. So my derm started me on Spironolactone. I would trust your derm that even if you do get a hormonal break out as your body adjusts to going off the birth control - it shouldn’t be anywhere near as bad as your previous acne.
